section.title: Restraint and Relationships
section.sectionRationale: This chapter sits inside the first great collection, the Proverbs of Solomon, 10:1 to 22:16, a long run of independent sentence proverbs. Chapter 17 keeps circling one seam: the restrained life, quiet, truthful, unretaliating, is stronger and safer than a life that grasps for advantage through strife, bribery, or a loose tongue.
section.thesis: Peace with a little is better than plenty won through quarreling, because the LORD tests every heart, rewards a guarded tongue and a loyal friend, and calls His people away from strife, favoritism, and retaliation toward quiet self-control.
section.frameNote: Seven clusters: peace over plenty and the LORD who tests hearts; words that heal or wound; the high cost of strife and crooked judgment; wisdom's worth and a friend who loves at all times; the heart under pressure; favoritism, bribery, and a grieving father; the wisdom of a closed mouth.

verses.text: Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife.
A wise servant will rule over a disgraceful son and share his inheritance as one of the brothers.
A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the {{bochan|tester}} of hearts.
A wicked man listens to evil lips; a liar gives ear to a destructive tongue.
He who mocks the poor insults their Maker; whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished.
Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of a son is his father.
Eloquent words are unfit for a fool; how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!
A bribe is a charm to its giver; wherever he turns, he succeeds.
Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but he who brings it up separates friends.
A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool.
An evil man seeks only rebellion; a cruel messenger will be sent against him.
It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a {{kesil|fool}} in his folly.
If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house.
To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out.
Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous, both are detestable to the LORD.

units.label: Wisdom's worth and a loyal friend
units.note: a friend loves at all times

verses.text: Why should the fool have money in his hand with no intention of buying wisdom?
A {{rea|friend}} loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
A man lacking judgment strikes hands in pledge and puts up security for his neighbor.
He who loves transgression loves strife; he who builds his gate high invites destruction.

units.label: The heart under pressure
units.note: grief, deceit, and a joyful heart

verses.text: The one with a perverse heart finds no good, and he whose tongue is deceitful falls into trouble.
A man fathers a fool to his own grief; the father of a fool has no joy.
A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones.
A wicked man takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice.
Wisdom is the focus of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth.
A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.
It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty.

units.label: The wisdom of a closed mouth

verses.text: A man of knowledge restrains his words, and a man of understanding maintains a calm spirit.
Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue.

bochan.gloss: Tester, prover, one who assays metal for purity. Verse 3 sets the smith's crucible and furnace beside the LORD, who tests hearts the way a refiner tests silver and gold, seeing past outward behavior to what a person truly loves.

kesil.gloss: Fool, the thickheaded, stubborn person who resists correction and lives by impulse rather than wisdom. Proverbs judges him more dangerous to confront than a wild animal robbed of her cubs, since a fool's folly is unpredictable and unreasoning.

rea.gloss: Friend, companion, neighbor, one bound to another by covenant loyalty rather than mere convenience. Verse 17 says this friend loves 'at all times,' constant through every season, a love the New Testament finds perfected in Christ.

basic.context: This chapter belongs to the long first collection of Solomon's proverbs, and it keeps circling one idea: restraint is strength. A dry morsel eaten in peace beats a feast torn apart by strife, a rebuke received humbly does more good than a hundred lashes on a fool, and a friend who loves at all times is worth more than money spent chasing wisdom you never intend to use.
basic.hermeneutics: These are general observations about wise living, not legal guarantees; not every dispute can be avoided and not every fool learns from rebuke. The proverbs describe how life usually rewards restraint and self-control and usually punishes strife, bribery, and retaliation, and they call the reader to choose the wise path even when results are not automatic.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD is called a bochan, a tester or refiner, who assays the heart the way a smith assays metal, verse 3. A kesil, a stubborn fool, is judged more dangerous to meet than a robbed bear, verse 12. And a rea, a covenant friend, loves at all times, verse 17, a love that anticipates the New Testament's picture of Christ as the friend who never lets go.
basic.typology: The friend who loves at all times and the brother born for adversity, verse 17, foreshadow Christ, the friend of sinners who lays down His life for those He loves. The LORD who tests hearts, verse 3, anticipates the final testing and vindication that comes only through Him who knew no sin.
basic.christ: Verse 17's friend who loves at all times finds its fullest answer in Jesus, who called His disciples friends and laid down His life for them, John 15:13 to 15. Where Proverbs 17 warns that returning evil for good never leaves a house, verse 13, Christ absorbed evil for good on the cross and broke that curse for all who trust Him.
basic.god: God is the tester of hearts, verse 3, who sees past behavior to motive, and He detests both acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous, verse 15, because He is just. Yet He is also the Maker whom the poor bear His image, verse 5, so mocking them is mocking Him; His justice and His compassion are inseparable.
basic.crossReferences: John 15:13 to 15 shows Christ as the friend who loves at all times and lays down His life. Romans 12:17 to 19 echoes the warning against repaying evil for evil. James 3 speaks to the restrained tongue. 1 Corinthians 4:5 points to the God who tests hearts and will bring hidden things to light.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 17 calls God's people to restraint, quiet contentment, loyal friendship, and a guarded tongue, because the LORD who tests every heart is not fooled by outward success won through strife. The whole story of Scripture answers this call in Jesus, the friend who loves at all times and whose peace is better than any feast bought with strife.

context.literary:
Proverbs 17 is built from short, loosely linked sayings, and its logic is clearest when read as a set of repeating motifs. The first is strife. It opens with a house full of feasting and strife, comes back to it in 'a flood' of quarrel in verse 14 and the lover of transgression who loves strife in verse 19, and it ends in two verses of silence. The chapter is therefore bracketed by noise and quiet, and the whole movement is from the quarreling house to the calm spirit.

The second motif is the fool. Eight verses mention one or a foolish son, 7, 10, 12, 16, 21, 24, 25 and 28, and each portrait adds a feature: unfit for fine speech, unmoved by rebuke, dangerous to meet, holding money with no intention of buying wisdom, a grief to his parents, looking everywhere except at what is near, and finally a figure who may pass for wise if he simply says nothing. The third motif is the family. Verse 2 speaks of a disgraceful son and a servant who inherits, verse 6 of grandchildren and fathers, and verses 21 and 25 of the father and mother of a fool, so the household forms a ring around the middle of the chapter.

At the centre stand sayings on friendship and security, verses 17 to 19, and on the heart, verses 20 to 22. Verse 3 acts as an anchor for the early part. It says that only the LORD can test a heart, the way silver is tested by a crucible, and that places every later saying about words and deeds under a judge who sees the motive. The chapter moves in a loose chain from the home, to courts and bribes, to friendships and pledges, to the inner life, and it comes round at the end to speech again.
context.historical:
Several sayings assume features of Israelite life that a modern reader can miss. Verse 1 speaks of a 'house full of feasting,' and the Hebrew behind that phrase, as the BSB footnote says, can also mean 'sacrifices.' In Israel the meat of a peace offering was shared by the worshipper's family and had to be eaten on the day it was offered, Leviticus 7:15. A house full of such meat was a house at its most festive. The proverb says that even that is worse than a dry crust where there is quiet. It touches the worship of Israel without naming it, since a shared meal before the LORD in a house of strife was a contradiction.

Verse 2 reflects inheritance customs. A son who shamed the family could lose his place, as Reuben lost the birthright, 1 Chronicles 5:1, and a loyal servant might become heir, as Abram feared in Genesis 15:2-3. Verse 18 reflects the practice of striking hands to guarantee another's debt, and debt could end in the loss of children to slavery, 2 Kings 4:1, which is why Proverbs warns against it repeatedly, Proverbs 6:1-3 and 22:26.

The courts of verses 15, 23 and 26 sat at the city gate, with elders who could be bribed. The Law banned it because a bribe blinds those who see, Exodus 23:8, and Deuteronomy 16:19. The 'hundred lashes' of verse 10 is hyperbole next to the Law's limit of forty, Deuteronomy 25:3. The bear of verse 12 was a real danger in the hills, and David's men are compared to one in 2 Samuel 17:8. The refiner's crucible of verse 3 belongs to the world of the smelter, where ore was heated until the impurities rose.
context.canonical:
Verse 3 is the center of a web of passages on testing. The psalmist says God has tested His people and refined them like silver, Psalm 66:10, Isaiah says He tested Israel in the furnace of affliction, Isaiah 48:10, and Zechariah and Malachi say He will refine them like silver and gold, Zechariah 13:9 and Malachi 3:3. Jeremiah gives the LORD's own words, 'I, the LORD, search the heart,' Jeremiah 17:10. Peter takes the picture to the church, where faith proved by fire is more precious than gold, 1 Peter 1:7, and Paul says the Lord will expose the motives of men's hearts, 1 Corinthians 4:5.

Verse 9 is paired with Proverbs 10:12, 'love covers all transgressions,' which Peter quotes, 1 Peter 4:8, and James extends to the one who turns a sinner from error, James 5:20. Verse 5 is cousin to Proverbs 14:31 and 22:2 and the confession of Job 31:15 that God made both servant and master. Verse 13 is lived out in David's house, where the sword never leaves after the death of Uriah, 2 Samuel 12:10, and countered by Paul's command not to repay evil for evil, Romans 12:17-19.

Verse 15 is the courtroom law of Exodus 23:7 and the prophet's woe on those who acquit the guilty for a bribe, Isaiah 5:23. Verse 17 resurfaces in Proverbs 18:24 and 27:10, and in the friendships of Jonathan and David, 1 Samuel 18:1, and Ruth and Naomi, Ruth 1:14. Verses 27 and 28 are met by Job's plea to his friends, Job 13:5, and James 1:19 and 3:2 in the New Testament.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage wanted his hearers to treat peace as a possession worth guarding at some cost. The opening verse puts a modest meal with quiet over a feast with conflict, and the rest of the chapter explains why: strife is a flood once released, a quarrelsome man opens a way for ruin, and a close friendship can be broken in a moment by repeating an old wrong. He asks the listener to value restraint in a culture where honor was often defended by loud words.

He also meant to protect the vulnerable. The warnings about bribes, the acquittal of the guilty and the flogging of the innocent were addressed to people who would one day sit in judgment, and the saying about mocking the poor reminds them whose workmanship the poor are. The poor are not to be a target of contempt, and the man who gloats over calamity has already taken a side against their Maker.

Finally, he meant to name the fool without cruelty. The chapter's portraits of fools show how foolishness looks, which is a protection to the learner. They also hold a door open: verse 16 asks why the fool has money in his hand and no mind to buy wisdom, which implies that wisdom can be bought and the price is willingness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
A good deal of the chapter is prescriptive by implication. Avoid the dispute before it breaks out, verse 14. Do not acquit the guilty or condemn the righteous, verse 15. Do not stand surety for a neighbour on impulse, verse 18. Hold your tongue when you have nothing wise to say, verses 27 and 28. These are directions for behavior, even though they are phrased as observations.

Other sayings describe, and the reader should not turn them into promises. Verse 13 says evil will not leave the house of one who repays good with evil, and this is how things tend to go, not a verdict on every family with trouble. Verse 22, that a joyful heart is good medicine, does not make illness a lack of cheer. Verse 21, that the father of a fool has no joy, is a statement of the grief such a father feels, not an accusation. Verse 28, that even a fool is thought wise if he keeps silent, is a remark about how silence is perceived. It does not praise silence everywhere. Proverbs 31:8 calls for speaking up for those who cannot, and Leviticus 19:17 tells us to rebuke a neighbor directly. The wisdom lies in knowing when to speak.

debates.question: Does verse 21, 'the father of a fool has no joy,' blame parents for how children turn out?

views.label: Yes, it is mainly about parental failure
views.case: Since Proverbs elsewhere commands parents to train children, verse 21 could be read as exposing bad parenting.

views.label: No, it describes grief without assigning blame
views.case: Wisdom literature consistently allows for children who reject good training, so the verse names painful reality rather than pronouncing verdict on parents; the emphasis falls on the child's foolish choices, not a formula for parental guilt.

debates.bearing: Read as description rather than blame, the proverb comforts grieving parents rather than condemning them, and keeps responsibility where Scripture places it, on the choices of the child as well as the parent.

debates.question: Does 'whoever conceals an offense promotes love' in verse 9 mean sin should be kept quiet?

views.label: Yes, love keeps wrongs private and does not rehearse them
views.case: The proverb sets 'conceals' against 'brings it up' and says the second separates friends. Proverbs 10:12 says love covers all transgressions, and Peter quotes it, 1 Peter 4:8. Proverbs 12:16 says a prudent man overlooks an insult. On this reading the ideal is a love that lets small injuries go and does not use an old wrong as a weapon.

views.label: No, covering means forgiving, not hiding serious sin
views.case: Verse 10 praises the rebuke that cuts deeply into a discerning man, and Leviticus 19:17 commands a direct rebuke so that guilt does not fall on you. Matthew 18:15 tells the wronged to go and confront privately. On this reading the verse is about not publicising a fault, while still bringing it to the person.

debates.bearing: The two readings fit together. The proverb forbids the gossip's use of a past offense, and it permits and even requires honest rebuke in private. Concealing serious harm that others will suffer, such as abuse or fraud, is not the love the verse commends. The test is whether the aim is repair, which is covering in the sense of forgiveness, or protection of the offender at the expense of the victim.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'feasting' of verse 1 is, literally, zivchê riv, 'sacrifices of strife,' as the BSB footnote notes. Zevach is the word for the sacrificial meal, so the saying pictures a table laden with the meat of worship in a house of conflict. The contrast between a worshipful meal and a quarreling heart is built into the Hebrew.

Verse 8 calls a bribe a 'charm,' and the Hebrew phrase is even-chen, literally a 'stone of favor.' The giver treats the bribe as a gem that wins approval wherever it is turned, and the proverb catches how bribery looks from the inside, as a lucky stone. Verse 23 then says the wicked man takes the bribe 'from the bosom,' as the footnote notes. The word for bosom, cheq, is the same word as the 'lap' into which the lot is cast in Proverbs 16:33. In one place the lap is where the LORD decides and in the other it is where justice is secretly bought.

In verse 9 the one who brings up an offense 'separates friends,' mafrid alluf. An alluf is a close companion, the person who is part of your inner life, and the same expression appears in Proverbs 16:28. The proverb thus treats gossip and grudge as the same act, a separation of intimates.

Verse 10 says a rebuke 'cuts into' a discerning man. The Hebrew verb is related to nachat, to go down, so the rebuke descends into him and sinks. It is a picture of correction that goes deep because he takes it in, while the fool is struck a hundred times and nothing sinks. Verse 14's 'release a flood' is literally 'one who lets out water,' the image of breaching a dam.

Verse 15 uses two forms of the courtroom verbs, the one who 'declares righteous' the guilty and the one who 'declares guilty' the righteous, matsdiq rasha and marshia tsaddiq. These are the verbs of a verdict, and both mean the judge has the facts reversed. The same verb for declaring righteous is behind Paul's phrase about God justifying the wicked, Romans 4:5, and this makes the verse a dramatic setting for the gospel. Verse 18 calls the one who pledges a man 'lacking judgment,' chasar-lev, literally 'lacking heart,' since in Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of understanding.

typology.type: The brother born for adversity, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: The proverb pictures a kinsman who shows up when trouble comes. Hebrews says the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family, so that Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers, Hebrews 2:11, and that He was made like His brothers in every way in order to be a merciful and faithful high priest, Hebrews 2:17. He was born into adversity for those He calls family. The proverb's friend and brother can stay with someone through trouble, but cannot remove its cause. Christ, who has been tempted in every way yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15, takes the trouble itself on Himself.

typology.type: The crucible and the furnace, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told that she had been refined in the furnace of affliction, Isaiah 48:10, and that testing exposed what was in her heart. Christ passes through the fire without dross. Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every way and was without sin, so the fire found nothing in Him to remove. For His people the furnace becomes the place where faith, more precious than gold, is proved, 1 Peter 1:7. The type has a limit: a crucible reveals impurities, and Christ's work does not stop at revealing them but removes them through His own sacrifice.

typology.type: Covering an offense in love, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The Psalms and Paul use the same picture of sin covered: blessed is he whose sins are covered, Psalm 32:1 and Romans 4:7. Human love can cover a small wrong by refusing to repeat it, as James 5:20 and 1 Peter 4:8 teach. Christ's covering costs more. The sin is not overlooked but atoned for, Hebrews 2:17, and is covered at the price of His blood, Romans 3:24-26. A parent or friend who forgives still leaves a debt. Christ pays it.

typology.type: Repaying evil with good, in contrast to verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The proverb warns that the one who returns evil for good will never be free of evil. David's house is the example, since he took Uriah's wife and Uriah's life in return for Uriah's loyalty, and the sword never left it, 2 Samuel 12:10. Jesus lives the reverse. On the cross He asks the Father to forgive the men who crucified Him, Luke 23:34, and Paul says that while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through His Son's death, Romans 5:10. The pattern that brought a curse on David's house becomes a blessing for those who receive Christ's mercy.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the Maker who was mocked. Verse 5 says whoever mocks the poor insults their Maker, and Colossians 1:16 says that all things were created through and for Christ. Then at the cross, passers-by heaped abuse on Him, and the chief priests and elders mocked Him, Matthew 27:39-44. The One through whom the poor were made became poor, and He was mocked as they are. The proverb takes on a force its author did not foresee: the Maker bore the insult.

It leads to Christ in the matter of the tested heart. The LORD who tests hearts, verse 3, came in the flesh, and He alone knows what is in a man, John 2:25. He was also the one heart that the furnace found pure. Because He has been tempted in every way yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15, He can sympathise with those who are tested and gives mercy to them.

It leads to Christ in verse 15, which is the most arresting link. The proverb says that acquitting the guilty is detestable to the LORD, and Exodus 23:7 has Him say, 'I will not acquit the guilty.' Yet Paul speaks of God as the one who justifies the wicked, Romans 4:5. The gospel looks at first like the thing the proverb condemns. Romans 3:24-26 shows how it is not: God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice so that He might be both just and the one who justifies. The guilty are not declared innocent by a careless judge. The penalty is borne, and 2 Corinthians 5:21 says God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf. That is why the justification of the ungodly can be righteous.

It leads to Christ in the silence of verses 27 and 28. A fool is thought wise when silent, but Christ's silence before Herod, Luke 23:9, and before Pilate, John 19:9, is not that of a fool. It is the silence of the servant who did not open His mouth, Isaiah 53:7, a restraint that held power in check.

And it leads to Christ in the joy and the crushed spirit of verse 22. Hebrews says that for the joy set before Him He endured the cross, Hebrews 12:2, and in Gethsemane His soul was consumed with sorrow to the point of death, Matthew 26:38. The sorrow crushed Him, and the joy outlasted it.

The caution: this is a chapter of wisdom for living, and its picture of the loyal friend, the quiet household and the cautious tongue does not hide a coded gospel. The links arise where the New Testament itself makes them.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who tests, and the testing is gentle in intent. The picture of the crucible says that He is the one who finds out what is in the heart and brings it to the surface for a purpose, as a refiner does with silver. He does not rely on outward results. That is why peace won through strife, or success won through a bribe, cannot satisfy Him, since He looks at the motive.

He is the Maker of the poor. Verse 5 puts the dignity of the poor under His own name, so that to mock them is to insult Him. Proverbs 14:31 and 22:2 say the same, and Job 31:15 adds that the same One formed both the servant and the master in the womb. God's regard for the poor is the ground of the chapter's whole ethic of justice.

He is a God of justice who hates verdicts turned upside down. Verse 15 says that acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous are both detestable to Him, and verse 23 and 26 condemn the bribe and the flogging of the innocent. Exodus 23:7 has Him say, 'I will not acquit the guilty.' His justice is not an optional extra of His character. It is the standard He sets for human judges.

He is also a God who loves at all times. The friend of verse 17 is not named as God, but the Bible calls Abraham the friend of God, James 2:23, and says the LORD spoke to Moses face to face as a man speaks to his friend, Exodus 33:11. The God who tests is also the God who draws near. He covers rather than exposes, as in Psalm 32:1, and the love that covers an offense, verse 9, is first His.

There is a tension in the chapter. God is the one who demands justice and abhors the acquittal of the guilty, yet the Bible says He justifies the ungodly. The resolution is in the cross, where He shows His righteousness and is the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:26. Neither His justice nor His mercy is reduced.

For worship, the chapter invites people to come to the God who sees through every offering and every pretext, and to find that being seen is also the way to being refined. It invites quiet too, since the God whose attention is on the heart does not need a flood of words, and Ecclesiastes 3:7 speaks of a time to be silent.

crossReferences.note: Paul rebukes the Corinthians because their gatherings for the Lord's Supper had divisions, with some eating well while others went hungry. It is verse 1 in the church: a shared meal of worship ruined by strife. The principle that a feast with conflict is worse than a crust in peace applied to the Lord's table.

The LORD says He will bring a remnant through the fire, refine them like silver and test them like gold. They will call on His name, and He will answer. The passage supplies the purpose behind verse 3's crucible: the testing leads to a people who belong to Him.

Peter says that the proven character of faith is more precious than gold that perishes, and that it results in praise, glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ. It takes the crucible of verse 3 and applies it to believers suffering trials, and gives the testing a goal.

Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, and whoever is kind to the needy honors Him. It is the positive side of verse 5. The same Maker is insulted by contempt and honored by kindness, so how we treat the poor is always a way of treating God.

Peter urges deep love among believers because love covers a multitude of sins, which echoes verse 9 and its source in Proverbs 10:12. In the church the principle becomes a daily habit: the readiness to forgive small offenses rather than keeping a list.

Nathan tells David that the sword will never depart from his house because he despised the LORD and took Uriah's wife. David had repaid Uriah's loyalty with death, and the rest of his reign is the working out of verse 13. The proverb is shown as history.

Paul tells believers not to repay anyone evil for evil, to live at peace as far as possible and to leave vengeance to God. It is the command to which verse 13 supplies the reason. The one who repays evil starts a cycle that does not stop, and the one who stops it leaves room for God.

The Law tells the judge to stay far from a false accusation and says, 'I will not acquit the guilty.' It is the legal source of verse 15 and shows that the proverb voices the character of God, which is why the cross had to settle how the guilty could be justified.

Job tells his friends that if they would only remain silent, that would be their wisdom. It is the voice of verse 28 spoken in pain: the friends had said much and understood little, and silence would have served Job better than their advice.

The souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan loved him as himself. It is the narrative picture of verse 17, a friendship that stayed constant when Jonathan's own father turned against David, and a friend who proved a brother in adversity.

In the peaceable kingdom the cow grazes with the bear and the wolf lives with the lamb. Verse 12 says it is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool. The new creation removes the danger of the bear, and the same promise reaches the human heart, since the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD, Isaiah 11:9.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a man who is alone in a good world, and God says it is not good, Genesis 2:18. Friendship and family are part of creation's design, and the chapter's concern for brothers, friends and households goes back to that. The first break comes quickly. Cain kills his brother Abel and asks whether he is his brother's keeper, Genesis 4:8-9. The picture of evil returned for good and a house that cannot be free of it runs through the story of Israel's families: Jacob's sons, David's household, and the kings.

The story is also one of testing. The refiner's fire is how Israel is described in the exile, Isaiah 48:10, and the prophets look beyond it to a people made pure, Zechariah 13:9. The Law's commands on bribes, honest courts and care for the poor set the standard against which the kings are measured, and almost every one falls short of it.

The gospel answers each part. The Maker of the poor comes as a poor man and is mocked. The friend who loves at all times lays down his life, and the brother born for adversity is born into it. The just judge acquits the guilty without ceasing to be just. The one who was silent before His accusers rises, and His peace becomes the possession of His people, John 14:27.

The new creation finishes what Proverbs 17 longs for. The feast that the LORD prepares for all peoples, Isaiah 25:6, is a feast with no strife in the house. The wolf lives with the lamb and the cow grazes with the bear, Isaiah 11:6-7. The tested are gathered, and the loyal friend and the brother are at the table together. The Lord who knows every heart will wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:4, and what the proverb called better than a feast, a quiet house, becomes the feast itself.

quiz.q: According to verse 1, what is better than a house full of feasting?

options.text: A dry morsel eaten in quietness, without strife.
options.note: Peace with little outweighs plenty torn apart by conflict.

options.text: A feast shared among many guests.
options.note: Feasting itself is not condemned; the issue is strife accompanying it.

options.text: A feast eaten alone in silence.
options.note: The verse contrasts quietness with strife, not company with solitude.

options.text: There is no comparison offered in the verse.
options.note: The verse is explicitly a 'better than' comparison.

quiz.q: What does verse 3 say the LORD does to hearts?

options.text: He tests them, as a crucible tests silver and a furnace tests gold.
options.note: The LORD is pictured as the tester or refiner of the heart's true metal.

options.text: He ignores the heart and judges only outward actions.
options.note: The verse specifically names the heart as what is tested, not merely behavior.

options.text: He hardens every heart without exception.
options.note: This misreads testing as hardening; the verse describes discernment, not fixed hardening.

options.text: He rewards hearts that appear silver or gold in color.
options.note: The metaphor of silver and gold is present but points to purity and value, not literal appearance.

quiz.q: What does verse 17 say about a true friend?

options.text: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
options.note: Constancy defines real friendship, especially in hardship.

options.text: A friend loves only when it is convenient.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's point about constancy.

options.text: A friend is mainly useful for business dealings.
options.note: The proverb speaks of love and adversity, not commercial usefulness.

options.text: A friend loves most of the time, but not during hardship.
options.note: Close, but it reverses the emphasis; adversity is precisely when this love proves real.

quiz.q: How does verse 13 describe the result of returning evil for good?

options.text: Evil will never leave that person's house.
options.note: Repaying good with evil brings lasting trouble on the offender.

options.text: It brings temporary trouble that quickly passes.
options.note: The verse's language is stronger and more lasting than 'temporary.'

options.text: It brings no consequence at all.
options.note: The verse explicitly warns of consequence, not immunity.

options.text: It only affects the person who was wronged.
options.note: The verse locates the consequence in the wrongdoer's own house, not merely the victim's.

quiz.q: What does the chapter commend about speech in verses 27 to 28?

options.text: Restraint: a knowledgeable person holds back words and even a fool seems wise if silent.
options.note: Verses 27 and 28 both praise restrained, calm speech.

options.text: Eloquence: speaking often and impressively.
options.note: The chapter elsewhere criticizes eloquent words wasted on fools, verse 7; the emphasis here is restraint, not eloquence.

options.text: Silence in every circumstance, never speaking.
options.note: Close, but the proverbs commend restraint and calm spirit, not an absolute vow of silence.

options.text: Loud confidence in speech.
options.note: This is the opposite of the calm, restrained spirit these verses commend.

questions: Verse 1 says a dry morsel in peace beats a feast full of strife. Where in your life are you tempted to chase more at the cost of peace?
The LORD is described as the tester of hearts, verse 3. What would He find if He tested the true motives behind your recent words or decisions?
A friend loves at all times, verse 17. Who has been that kind of friend to you, and who might need you to be that kind of friend to them this week?
Verse 13 warns that repaying evil for good brings lasting trouble. Is there a grudge or a tit for tat pattern you are holding onto that this proverb calls you to release?
Verses 27 and 28 praise restrained speech. What would change in your closest relationship if you held your tongue for one extra breath before responding?

translationNotes.note: Bochan, rendered 'tester,' pictures a metallurgist assaying ore; some translations render it 'prover' or 'refiner,' each capturing the same image of testing for purity.
'To start a quarrel is to release a flood' translates an image of breaching a dam; once released, a quarrel is very hard to contain again.
'A joyful heart is good medicine' can also be rendered 'does good like a medicine,' underscoring that emotional health has bodily effect, an idea the Hebrew ties closely to the body's 'bones.'
